questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which branch of agriculture is concerned mainly with the cultivation of crops?
options: Agricultural economics
Crop production
Agricultural extension
Animal science
questions.explanation: Crop production (agronomy) deals specifically with the growing, management, and harvesting of crops, distinct from livestock, economics, or extension work.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which branch of agriculture deals with the study of soils and their management for crop growth?
options: Animal science
Forestry
Soil science
Fishery
questions.explanation: Soil science (pedology/edaphology) focuses on soil formation, properties, and fertility management to support plant growth.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The branch of agriculture that studies the breeding, feeding, and management of livestock is called
options: animal science
agric economics
horticulture
agricultural extension
questions.explanation: Animal science covers the husbandry of farm animals, including their breeding, nutrition, and health management.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agricultural economics is best described as the branch of agriculture concerned with
options: the breeding of improved livestock
the control of crop pests
the classification of soils
the efficient allocation of farm resources and farm business management
questions.explanation: Agricultural economics applies economic principles to farming, covering resource allocation, farm management, costs, and profitability.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agricultural extension is primarily concerned with
options: the direct sale of farm produce to consumers
transferring research findings and improved techniques to farmers
the breeding of disease-resistant crop varieties
the surveying of farmland boundaries
questions.explanation: Extension work bridges the gap between agricultural researchers and farmers by educating farmers on improved practices.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Forestry, as a branch of agriculture, is mainly concerned with
options: the rearing of fish in ponds
the management and conservation of trees and forest resources
the processing of dairy products
the cultivation of vegetables only
questions.explanation: Forestry involves the planting, management, and conservation of trees for timber, fuelwood, and environmental protection.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Fishery, as a branch of agriculture, deals mainly with
options: the culture, management, and harvesting of fish and other aquatic organisms
the classification of farm tools
the breeding of poultry only
the study of soil horizons
questions.explanation: Fishery (aquaculture and capture fisheries) focuses on producing and harvesting fish and other aquatic life for food and income.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Horticulture is the branch of agriculture concerned mainly with the cultivation of
options: fruits, vegetables, and ornamental plants
forest trees for timber only
farm animals
cereal crops only
questions.explanation: Horticulture deals with the intensive cultivation of fruits, vegetables, flowers, and ornamentals, distinct from broad-acre crop farming.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agricultural mechanization refers to the branch of agriculture concerned with
options: the use of machines and equipment to carry out farm operations
the breeding of new crop varieties
the marketing of farm produce
the study of soil chemistry
questions.explanation: Mechanization involves applying engineering and machinery, such as tractors and implements, to improve efficiency in farm operations.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Subsistence agriculture is best described as farming practised mainly to
options: supply raw materials to large agro-industries
produce only cash crops for the international market
produce food primarily for the farmer's family with little surplus for sale
generate maximum profit through large-scale exports
questions.explanation: Subsistence agriculture is small-scale farming aimed at feeding the household rather than generating significant commercial profit.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Commercial agriculture is characterised mainly by
options: the total absence of modern inputs
farming on very small plots of land only
farming only for household consumption
large-scale production of crops or livestock primarily for sale and profit
questions.explanation: Commercial agriculture involves large-scale, market-oriented production, often using modern inputs and mechanization to maximise profit.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is a major problem hindering agricultural development in developing countries?
options: Excess availability of agricultural credit
Too many trained extension agents
Poor land tenure system that restricts access to farmland
Over-abundance of storage facilities
questions.explanation: Insecure or fragmented land tenure discourages long-term investment in land and limits farmers' access to adequate farmland.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Inadequate agricultural finance is a major constraint to agricultural development mainly because it
options: reduces the need for storage facilities
limits farmers' ability to purchase inputs, equipment, and hire labour
eliminates the need for farm labour
increases the fertility of the soil
questions.explanation: Without adequate credit or capital, farmers cannot afford improved seeds, fertilisers, equipment, and labour needed to boost productivity.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Poor transportation network is a problem of agricultural development mainly because it
options: makes it difficult to move farm produce from rural farms to urban markets, causing post-harvest losses
has no effect on farm produce marketing
increases the shelf life of perishable produce
reduces the cost of farm inputs
questions.explanation: Bad roads and limited transport delay produce reaching markets, leading to spoilage of perishable crops and reduced farmer income.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Inadequate storage and processing facilities contribute to agricultural underdevelopment mainly by causing
options: a reduction in the need for agricultural credit
improved quality of stored grains
high post-harvest losses of farm produce
an increase in the market value of produce
questions.explanation: Without proper storage or processing, harvested crops deteriorate quickly, leading to significant losses in quantity and quality.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Inadequate agricultural extension services hinder agricultural development mainly because farmers
options: receive too much government subsidy
have excess access to modern machinery
are unable to grow any crops at all
do not receive timely information on improved farming techniques
questions.explanation: Without sufficient extension contact, farmers continue to use outdated methods and miss out on innovations that could raise yields.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Environmental degradation, such as erosion and deforestation, affects agricultural development mainly by
options: improving water infiltration in all soils
eliminating the need for soil conservation
reducing soil fertility and the long-term productive capacity of land
increasing the amount of arable land available
questions.explanation: Degradation processes strip away fertile topsoil and vegetation cover, reducing land's capacity to support productive agriculture.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agricultural land use refers to the
options: use of land for building residential estates only
construction of roads and industries only
mining of mineral resources
allocation of land specifically for farming activities such as crop and livestock production
questions.explanation: Agricultural land use covers land devoted to crop cultivation, animal rearing, forestry, and fishery, as opposed to non-agricultural uses.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of non-agricultural land use?
options: Construction of residential buildings and roads
Rearing of cattle and poultry
Cultivation of maize and cassava
Establishment of a fish pond
questions.explanation: Non-agricultural land use includes activities like housing, road construction, and industry, which do not involve crop or livestock production.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Under the communal land tenure system, land is mainly
options: owned collectively by the community and allocated to members for use
owned by a single individual with full rights to sell
inherited exclusively through a will
leased from government for a fixed number of years
questions.explanation: In communal tenure, land belongs to the whole community (often through the traditional ruler or family head), who allocate portions to members for farming.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Under the individual (freehold) land tenure system, a person
options: holds full ownership rights over the land and can sell, lease, or bequeath it
must share the land equally with all community members
has no right to transfer the land to another person
can only use the land for a fixed short-term lease
questions.explanation: Individual or freehold tenure grants the landholder full and permanent ownership rights, including the right to sell or transfer the land.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Leasehold land tenure system allows a person to
options: use land for a specified period under agreed terms, after paying rent to the owner
use the land freely without any form of agreement
own the land permanently without any conditions
inherit the land automatically from a deceased relative
questions.explanation: Under leasehold, the tenant is granted the right to use land for a fixed term, usually against payment of rent to the actual landowner.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Inheritance as a land tenure system involves land being
options: purchased outright from the government
passed down from one generation to another within a family
leased annually from a private company
seized by the state for public use
questions.explanation: Inheritance tenure transfers land ownership through succession, typically from parents to children, within the family lineage.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A major aim of the Nigerian Land Use Act of 1978 was to
options: eliminate all forms of land taxation permanently
abolish agriculture completely in Nigeria
make land more easily accessible for agricultural and other development purposes
transfer all land ownership to foreign investors
questions.explanation: The Land Use Act vested land in state governors to simplify land acquisition and reduce disputes, aiming to ease access to land for development, including agriculture.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: One merit of the Land Use Act is that it
options: increases the fragmentation of farmland
abolishes the need for any government administration of land
reduces land tenure disputes by vesting control of land in the state government
guarantees free land to every citizen without conditions
questions.explanation: By centralising land control under state governors, the Act aimed to minimise conflicting claims and disputes over land ownership.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A major demerit of the Land Use Act is that it
options: makes land ownership completely free of any documentation
gives farmers unlimited rights to sell communal land
involves bureaucratic delays and costs in obtaining a certificate of occupancy
has increased the amount of land available to every farmer automatically
questions.explanation: In practice, the Act's requirement for governor's consent and certificates of occupancy has often led to slow, costly bureaucratic processes.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agricultural ecology is best defined as the study of
options: the relationship between living organisms and their environment in agricultural systems
the design of farm machinery
the chemical composition of fertilisers
the marketing of farm produce
questions.explanation: Agricultural ecology examines how crops, livestock, and other organisms interact with each other and with their physical environment on the farm.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Biotic components of the agricultural environment include
options: wind speed and humidity only
soil texture and soil structure only
rainfall, temperature, and solar radiation
pests, weeds, predators, parasites, and soil microorganisms
questions.explanation: Biotic components are the living factors in the environment, including pests, weeds, predators, parasites, and microorganisms, as opposed to abiotic (non-living) factors.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Abiotic components of the agricultural environment include
options: climatic factors such as rainfall and temperature, and edaphic (soil) factors
weeds and pests
soil microorganisms only
predators and parasites
questions.explanation: Abiotic components are the non-living physical and chemical factors, including climate (rainfall, temperature, light) and soil (edaphic) properties.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Predators affect agricultural production mainly by
options: feeding on and reducing the population of pests or other organisms
adding organic matter to the soil directly
fixing atmospheric nitrogen in the soil
improving soil aeration through burrowing only
questions.explanation: Predators hunt and consume other organisms (often crop pests), which can help naturally regulate pest populations on the farm.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Parasites in agricultural ecology are organisms that
options: only feed on decaying organic matter
live on or in a host organism and derive nourishment at the host's expense
manufacture their own food through photosynthesis
live independently without affecting other organisms
questions.explanation: Parasites depend on a host for nutrients, often harming the host in the process, as seen with many crop and livestock diseases and pests.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Soil microorganisms, such as bacteria and fungi, benefit agriculture mainly by
options: reducing the water-holding capacity of soil
competing directly with crops for sunlight
increasing soil erosion
decomposing organic matter and releasing nutrients for plant uptake
questions.explanation: Soil microorganisms break down organic residues into simpler compounds, releasing essential nutrients that become available to growing plants.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Weeds are considered harmful biotic components mainly because they
options: serve as the primary food source for livestock only
add valuable nitrogen directly to the soil
compete with crops for water, nutrients, light, and space
improve soil structure more effectively than crops
questions.explanation: Weeds grow alongside crops and compete for the same essential growth resources, thereby reducing crop yield if not controlled.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Mutualism is a type of relationship between organisms in which
options: both organisms are harmed by the association
one organism benefits while the other is unaffected
one organism benefits while the other is harmed
both organisms benefit from the association
questions.explanation: Mutualism is a symbiotic relationship where both partners gain benefit, such as nitrogen-fixing bacteria and leguminous plants.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Commensalism is a relationship between two organisms in which
options: one organism is harmed while the other is unaffected
one organism benefits while the other is neither helped nor harmed
both organisms benefit equally
both organisms compete for the same resource
questions.explanation: In commensalism, only one party gains an advantage from the relationship, while the other experiences no significant effect.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Parasitism as an ecological relationship results in
options: neither organism being affected
the parasite benefiting while the host is harmed
the host benefiting while the parasite is harmed
both organisms benefiting equally
questions.explanation: Parasitism is a relationship where the parasite gains nutrients and often causes harm or disease to the host organism.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Competition in agricultural ecology occurs when organisms
options: have no interaction with one another at all
live together without needing any shared resources
struggle for the same limited resources such as light, water, and nutrients
cooperate to obtain resources for mutual benefit
questions.explanation: Competition arises when two or more organisms, such as crops and weeds, require the same limited resources, negatively affecting one or both.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Rainfall, as an environmental factor, affects crop production mainly by
options: determining the market price of produce
determining the amount of water available for plant growth and influencing crop choice
changing the colour of harvested produce
affecting only the taste of livestock feed
questions.explanation: The quantity and distribution of rainfall directly affect water availability for crops, influencing which crops thrive in a given area.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Temperature, as an environmental factor, mainly affects crops and livestock by influencing
options: the political boundaries of a farm
the type of land tenure practised in an area
the rate of physiological processes such as photosynthesis, respiration, and growth
the shape of farm buildings
questions.explanation: Temperature directly affects metabolic processes in living organisms, with each species having an optimal range for normal growth and productivity.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Solar radiation (sunlight) is important to crop production mainly because it provides the energy needed for
options: nitrogen fixation only
photosynthesis
soil erosion control
mineral weathering only
questions.explanation: Sunlight supplies the energy that green plants use during photosynthesis to manufacture their own food, essential for growth.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Wind, as an environmental factor, can affect agriculture negatively mainly by
options: improving the water-holding capacity of soil
eliminating the need for pollination in crops
causing lodging of crops and increasing the rate of soil erosion
increasing soil fertility permanently
questions.explanation: Strong winds can physically damage crops by causing them to fall over (lodging) and can also strip away exposed topsoil, causing erosion.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: High relative humidity in the environment tends to favour
options: the complete prevention of plant diseases
a reduction in transpiration rate to zero
a decrease in insect pest populations only
the development and spread of fungal and bacterial crop diseases
questions.explanation: Humid conditions create a favourable environment for the growth and spread of many fungal and bacterial pathogens affecting crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Agro-allied industries are best described as industries that
options: manufacture only farm machinery and tools
depend on agricultural produce as raw materials for their operations
provide only extension services to farmers
focus solely on banking services for farmers
questions.explanation: Agro-allied (agro-based) industries process farm produce into finished or semi-finished goods, relying directly on agriculture for raw materials.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The soap-making industry depends mainly on which agricultural raw material?
options: Cotton lint
Oilseeds, such as palm kernel and groundnut
Hides and skins
Cocoa beans
questions.explanation: Oils extracted from oilseeds like palm kernel and groundnut serve as key raw materials in the manufacture of soap.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The paper and pulp industry depends mainly on which agricultural raw material?
options: Hides and skins
Cocoa beans
Cotton lint
Pulpwood from forest trees
questions.explanation: Pulpwood harvested from forest plantations is processed into wood pulp, the primary raw material used in paper manufacturing.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The beverage industry (producing drinks such as chocolate and tea beverages) depends mainly on
options: cocoa and tea leaves
pulpwood
cotton lint
hides and skins
questions.explanation: Cocoa beans and tea leaves are processed into beverages such as chocolate drinks and tea, forming the base raw material for this agro-allied sector.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The textile industry depends mainly on which agricultural raw material?
options: Cocoa
Palm kernel
Cotton
Pulpwood
questions.explanation: Cotton fibre (lint) is spun into yarn and woven into fabric, making it the principal raw material for the textile industry.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The leather industry depends mainly on which agricultural raw material?
options: Cocoa beans
Oilseeds
Pulpwood
Hides and skins from livestock
questions.explanation: Hides (from cattle) and skins (from goats/sheep) are tanned and processed to produce leather used in footwear, bags, and other products.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Rocks are broken down into smaller particles to form soil mainly through the process of
options: weathering
photosynthesis
fermentation
combustion
questions.explanation: Weathering, whether physical, chemical, or biological, breaks down parent rock into smaller fragments and minerals that eventually form soil.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Physical (mechanical) weathering breaks down rocks mainly through
options: the decomposition of organic matter
the chemical action of acids on minerals
temperature changes causing expansion and contraction, and frost action
the activity of soil bacteria
questions.explanation: Physical weathering disintegrates rock through processes like alternating heating/cooling and freeze-thaw cycles, without changing the rock's chemical composition.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Chemical weathering breaks down rocks mainly through processes such as
options: the burrowing activity of earthworms
hydrolysis, oxidation, and carbonation
frost action and temperature changes only
the grazing activity of livestock
questions.explanation: Chemical weathering alters the mineral composition of rocks through reactions like hydrolysis, oxidation, and carbonation, breaking them down over time.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Biological weathering of rocks occurs mainly through the activities of
options: chemical reactions with rainwater only
wind erosion alone
volcanic eruptions
plant roots and burrowing organisms that break rocks apart
questions.explanation: Living organisms, such as plant roots growing into cracks and burrowing animals, physically and chemically contribute to breaking down rock material.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Igneous rocks are formed mainly from the
options: compaction and cementation of sediments
cooling and solidification of molten magma or lava
accumulation of decomposed organic matter
transformation of existing rocks under heat and pressure
questions.explanation: Igneous rocks, such as granite and basalt, form when molten magma or lava cools and solidifies, either below or on the earth's surface.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Sedimentary rocks are formed mainly through the
options: deposition, compaction, and cementation of sediments over time
melting and recrystallisation of existing rock
cooling and solidification of magma
combustion of organic material
questions.explanation: Sedimentary rocks, such as sandstone and limestone, form as layers of sediment accumulate and are compressed and cemented together over long periods.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Metamorphic rocks are formed when existing rocks are
options: deposited as loose sediment on the ocean floor
dissolved completely in water
cooled rapidly from a molten state
subjected to intense heat and pressure, altering their structure and mineral composition
questions.explanation: Metamorphic rocks, such as marble and slate, form when existing igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic rocks are transformed by heat and pressure without melting completely.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following factors influences the rate and type of soil formation?
options: Parent material, climate, living organisms, topography, and time
Only the market value of the land
Only the political ownership of the land
Only the colour of the parent rock
questions.explanation: Soil formation (pedogenesis) is influenced by the interacting factors of parent material, climate, organisms, relief/topography, and time.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: In a typical soil profile, the topsoil, rich in organic matter and most biological activity, is referred to as the
options: C horizon
A horizon
B horizon
D horizon (bedrock)
questions.explanation: The A horizon (topsoil) is the uppermost layer, characterised by high organic matter content and intense biological activity.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The subsoil layer of a soil profile, which typically has less organic matter but accumulated minerals leached from above, is called the
options: O horizon
R horizon (bedrock)
B horizon
A horizon
questions.explanation: The B horizon, or subsoil, often accumulates clay, iron, and other minerals leached down from the topsoil above it.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The soil horizon consisting of partially weathered parent material, lying just above the unweathered bedrock, is the
options: B horizon
A horizon
C horizon
O horizon
questions.explanation: The C horizon consists of weathered parent rock material that has not yet developed the properties of true soil found in the A and B horizons.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The unweathered parent rock underlying the soil profile is referred to as the
options: B horizon
D horizon (bedrock)
A horizon
O horizon
questions.explanation: The D horizon (or R horizon) is the solid, unweathered bedrock from which the overlying soil horizons ultimately develop.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Soil texture refers to the
options: depth of the soil profile
chemical reaction (pH) of the soil
arrangement of soil particles into aggregates
relative proportion of sand, silt, and clay particles in a soil
questions.explanation: Soil texture describes the proportion of differently sized mineral particles, which affects water movement, aeration, and nutrient retention.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Soil structure refers to the
options: arrangement of soil particles into aggregates or crumbs
temperature of the soil at different depths
amount of organic matter present in a soil
proportion of sand, silt, and clay in the soil
questions.explanation: Soil structure describes how individual particles bind together into aggregates, which influences porosity, drainage, and root penetration.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Soil porosity refers to the
options: colour of the soil at the surface
total weight of a given volume of soil
acidity or alkalinity of the soil
proportion of the soil volume occupied by pore spaces (air and water)
questions.explanation: Porosity is the fraction of soil volume made up of pore spaces, which hold the air and water essential for plant roots and soil organisms.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The water-holding capacity of a soil refers to its ability to
options: retain water against the pull of gravity for use by plants
convert water into soil minerals
allow water to drain away immediately
prevent any water from entering the soil
questions.explanation: Water-holding capacity describes how much water a soil can retain in its pore spaces for later uptake by plant roots.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Capillarity in soil refers to the
options: chemical breakdown of soil minerals
downward movement of water under gravity alone
loss of water from the soil surface through evaporation
upward or lateral movement of water through small soil pores due to surface tension
questions.explanation: Capillary action moves water through fine soil pores against gravity, helping to redistribute moisture within the soil profile.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Soil pH is a measure of the
options: acidity or alkalinity of the soil
water-holding capacity of the soil
total mineral content of the soil
amount of organic matter in the soil
questions.explanation: Soil pH indicates the concentration of hydrogen ions, showing whether a soil is acidic, neutral, or alkaline, which affects nutrient availability.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is a soil macro-organism important in improving soil aeration and structure?
options: Fungus
Earthworm
Bacteria
Virus
questions.explanation: Earthworms are macro-organisms whose burrowing activity improves soil aeration, drainage, and structure while also mixing organic matter into the soil.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Termites, as soil macro-organisms, affect the soil mainly by
options: burrowing and building mounds that alter soil structure and aeration
fixing atmospheric nitrogen directly
photosynthesising to produce food
decomposing rocks chemically
questions.explanation: Termite activity, including tunnelling and mound-building, physically alters soil structure, aeration, and drainage patterns.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Soil microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi contribute to soil fertility mainly by
options: competing with crops for sunlight
reducing soil porosity permanently
decomposing organic matter and releasing plant nutrients
increasing soil erosion
questions.explanation: Microbial decomposition breaks down organic residues into simpler forms, releasing essential nutrients back into the soil for plant use.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is classified as a macro-nutrient required by plants in relatively large quantities?
options: Boron
Molybdenum
Zinc
Nitrogen
questions.explanation: Nitrogen, along with phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, and sulphur, is a macro-nutrient needed by plants in large amounts, unlike micro-nutrients such as zinc.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is classified as a micro-nutrient required by plants in very small quantities?
options: Zinc
Potassium
Nitrogen
Phosphorus
questions.explanation: Zinc, along with iron, molybdenum, cobalt, boron, and copper, is a micro-nutrient needed only in trace amounts, unlike macro-nutrients like nitrogen.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Nitrogen deficiency in plants is commonly indicated by
options: abnormally rapid fruit ripening
excessive dark green colouration of leaves
purpling of leaves only
yellowing of leaves (chlorosis), especially older leaves, and stunted growth
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is essential for chlorophyll and protein synthesis, so its deficiency typically causes yellowing of older leaves and poor, stunted growth.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Necrosis, a symptom of certain nutrient deficiencies in plants, refers to the
options: excessive greening of young leaves
increased root branching
abnormal elongation of stems
death of plant tissue, often appearing as brown or black patches
questions.explanation: Necrosis is the death of plant cells and tissue, commonly appearing as dead brown or black spots on leaves due to certain nutrient deficiencies.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Stunted growth in plants, often resulting from phosphorus deficiency, refers to
options: unusually rapid and excessive vegetative growth
abnormally reduced or slowed plant growth and development
premature flowering of the plant
an increase in leaf size beyond normal
questions.explanation: Phosphorus is vital for energy transfer and root development, so its deficiency commonly results in stunted, poorly developed plants.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The nitrogen cycle process in which atmospheric nitrogen gas is converted into ammonia by certain bacteria is called
options: nitrification
denitrification
nitrogen fixation
ammonification
questions.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, such as Rhizobium in legume root nodules, convert inert atmospheric nitrogen gas into ammonia usable by plants.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The carbon cycle mainly describes the movement of carbon between the
options: atmosphere, living organisms, and the soil/oceans
atmosphere and outer space
soil and rocks only
farm machinery and farm buildings
questions.explanation: The carbon cycle traces how carbon moves through photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, and combustion among the atmosphere, organisms, soil, and oceans.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The phosphorus cycle differs from the nitrogen and carbon cycles mainly in that phosphorus
options: exists mainly as a gas in the atmosphere
has no significant gaseous phase and cycles mainly through soil, water, and organisms
is fixed only by bacteria in root nodules
cannot be taken up by plant roots at all
questions.explanation: Unlike nitrogen and carbon, phosphorus lacks a significant atmospheric gas form and instead cycles primarily through rock weathering, soil, water, and living organisms.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The water cycle (hydrological cycle) mainly involves the continuous movement of water through
options: photosynthesis and respiration only
mineral weathering of rocks alone
evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and infiltration/runoff
nitrogen fixation and denitrification
questions.explanation: The water cycle describes water's continuous movement between the atmosphere, land, and oceans through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and runoff/infiltration.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Crop rotation helps maintain soil fertility mainly by
options: permanently exhausting the soil of all nutrients
increasing soil erosion on the farm
eliminating the need for any soil management
alternating crops with different nutrient demands and disrupting pest/disease cycles
questions.explanation: By rotating crops with differing nutrient needs (e.g., cereals following legumes), farmers help balance soil nutrients and break pest and disease cycles.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Green manuring involves
options: ploughing under a growing green crop to decompose and enrich the soil with organic matter
applying synthetic nitrogen fertiliser to the soil
spreading dried animal dung on the soil surface
removing all vegetation from the field before planting
questions.explanation: Green manure crops are grown and then ploughed into the soil while still green, adding organic matter and nutrients as they decompose.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Farmyard manure is best described as
options: a mixture of animal dung, urine, and bedding material used to fertilise soil
a herbicide used to control weeds
a synthetic chemical fertiliser applied in granular form
a type of soil found only in river valleys
questions.explanation: Farmyard manure is an organic fertiliser composed of decomposed animal waste and bedding, enriching soil with nutrients and organic matter.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Compost is produced mainly through the
options: crushing of parent rock into fine particles
chemical synthesis of nitrogen fertiliser
mining of mineral deposits from the earth
controlled decomposition of plant and animal waste materials
questions.explanation: Composting is the deliberate, controlled breakdown of organic waste (crop residues, kitchen waste, manure) into a nutrient-rich soil conditioner.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Broadcasting, as a method of fertiliser application, involves
options: spraying fertiliser solution onto the leaves of plants
scattering fertiliser evenly over the entire field surface
applying fertiliser directly around the base of each plant only
placing fertiliser in a narrow band beside the crop row
questions.explanation: Broadcasting spreads fertiliser uniformly across the whole field, suitable for crops planted closely together or before land preparation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Banding, as a method of fertiliser application, involves
options: mixing fertiliser into irrigation water only
spraying fertiliser as a fine mist onto plant leaves
scattering fertiliser randomly over the whole field
placing fertiliser in a narrow strip beside or below the seed/crop row
questions.explanation: Banding places fertiliser in a concentrated strip near the seed or plant row, making nutrients readily accessible to developing roots while reducing waste.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Ring application, a method of fertiliser placement, is commonly used for
options: cereal crops planted in rows
crops grown in a nursery seedbed only
crops irrigated by sprinklers only
tree crops, where fertiliser is applied in a circle around the base of the tree
questions.explanation: Ring application places fertiliser in a circular band around the drip line of a tree, matching the area where feeder roots are most active.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Foliar application of fertiliser involves
options: spraying a nutrient solution directly onto the leaves of plants
burying fertiliser deep within the soil profile
broadcasting fertiliser granules over bare soil
mixing fertiliser into farmyard manure before application
questions.explanation: Foliar feeding delivers nutrients in liquid form directly to plant leaves, allowing for rapid absorption, especially useful for correcting micronutrient deficiencies.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Fallowing, as a soil fertility management practice, involves
options: irrigating the land throughout the year
leaving land uncultivated for a period to allow natural regeneration of fertility
applying chemical fertiliser every planting season
continuously cropping the land without any rest period
questions.explanation: Fallowing rests the land, allowing natural vegetation to regrow and organic matter and nutrients to be restored before the land is cultivated again.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Liming is a soil fertility management practice carried out mainly to
options: reduce soil acidity and raise the soil pH
add nitrogen directly to the soil
improve soil drainage in sandy soils only
increase the acidity of alkaline soils
questions.explanation: Applying lime (calcium compounds) neutralises excess soil acidity, raising the pH to a range that favours nutrient availability for most crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Cover-cropping helps maintain soil fertility mainly by
options: removing all organic matter from the soil
exposing bare soil to direct sunlight and rainfall
increasing the rate of soil erosion
protecting the soil surface from erosion and adding organic matter when incorporated
questions.explanation: Cover crops shield the soil from erosive rainfall and wind, suppress weeds, and add organic matter to the soil when ploughed under.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Organic farming is a farming system that relies mainly on
options: natural inputs such as organic manure and biological pest control, avoiding synthetic chemicals
large-scale mechanised irrigation only
genetically modified seeds only
the exclusive use of synthetic fertilisers and pesticides
questions.explanation: Organic farming avoids synthetic fertilisers and pesticides, relying instead on natural soil fertility practices and biological pest management.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Overhead irrigation supplies water to crops mainly by
options: allowing water to flow along furrows between crop rows
flooding the entire field until saturated
spraying water over the crop from above, similar to rainfall
supplying water directly to the root zone below the soil surface
questions.explanation: Overhead (sprinkler) irrigation distributes water through pipes and sprinklers above the crop canopy, mimicking natural rainfall.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Surface irrigation supplies water to crops mainly by
options: supplying water directly below the root zone through buried pipes
allowing water to flow over the soil surface, such as in furrows or basins
misting the leaves of the crop only
spraying water above the crop canopy
questions.explanation: Surface irrigation methods, such as furrow or basin irrigation, apply water directly onto the soil surface, allowing it to spread and infiltrate.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Subsurface irrigation supplies water to crops mainly by
options: relying solely on natural rainfall
spraying water above the crop from overhead sprinklers
flooding the entire surface of the field
delivering water directly below the soil surface near the plant root zone
questions.explanation: Subsurface irrigation uses buried pipes or channels to supply water directly to the root zone, minimising surface evaporation losses.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Waterlogging, a common problem associated with poor irrigation practices, refers to
options: an increase in soil salinity only
insufficient water supply to meet crop needs
excessive accumulation of water in the soil, depriving roots of oxygen
excessive drainage of water from the soil
questions.explanation: Waterlogging occurs when soil pores become saturated with water, excluding air and depriving plant roots of the oxygen needed for respiration.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Soil salinity, a problem often associated with poor irrigation practices in dry areas, refers to
options: the accumulation of excess organic matter in the soil
an increase in beneficial soil microorganisms
an increase in the soil's water-holding capacity
the accumulation of excess soluble salts in the soil, harmful to most crops
questions.explanation: Poor irrigation, especially with inadequate drainage, can cause salts to accumulate in the soil as water evaporates, harming most crop plants.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Surface drainage removes excess water from farmland mainly by
options: channelling water away through open ditches or graded surface channels
pumping water up from a deep underground reservoir
installing buried perforated pipes below the root zone
spraying water into the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Surface drainage uses open ditches, channels, or graded land to direct excess surface water away from the field.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Subsurface drainage removes excess water from farmland mainly by
options: digging open ditches across the field surface
using buried perforated pipes or tiles to carry away excess water below the soil surface
spraying water onto the crop canopy
increasing the salinity of the soil
questions.explanation: Subsurface drainage systems use underground perforated pipes (tile drains) to collect and remove excess water from within the soil profile.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A cutlass (machete) is mainly used on the farm for
options: measuring the pH of soil
deep ploughing of large fields
irrigating crops
clearing vegetation and harvesting some crops
questions.explanation: The cutlass is a simple hand tool with a sharp blade, commonly used to clear bush, cut grass, and harvest certain crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: An axe is mainly used on the farm for
options: weeding between crop rows
felling trees and splitting wood
spraying pesticides
digging planting holes
questions.explanation: The axe has a heavy blade designed for chopping down trees and splitting logs, tasks not suited to lighter tools like the cutlass or hoe.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A hoe is a simple farm tool used mainly for
options: felling large trees
weeding, making ridges, and light tillage
measuring farmland boundaries
harvesting tree crops from a height
questions.explanation: The hoe's flat blade is used for shallow cultivation tasks such as weeding, making ridges or mounds, and light soil turning.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A spade is mainly used on the farm for
options: cutting down standing trees
digging and turning small areas of soil
spraying chemicals over crops
surveying farmland distances
questions.explanation: The spade has a flat, sharp-edged blade suited for digging planting holes, turning soil, and other small-scale digging tasks.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A shovel differs from a spade mainly in that a shovel is designed primarily for
options: measuring soil moisture
cutting through tree roots
lifting and moving loose materials such as soil, sand, or manure
precise digging of narrow trenches
questions.explanation: While a spade is optimised for digging and cutting into soil, a shovel's broader, curved blade is better suited for scooping and moving loose material.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A rake is a simple farm tool used mainly for
options: harvesting root crops
felling trees for timber
digging deep planting holes
gathering leaves, debris, and levelling loose soil
questions.explanation: The rake's tined head is designed to gather loose material like leaves and crop residue, and to smooth and level the soil surface.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Proper maintenance of simple farm tools, such as cleaning and oiling after use, is important mainly to
options: prevent rusting and prolong the tool's useful life
reduce the sharpness of the blade
increase the purchase price of the tool
make the tool heavier for better balance
questions.explanation: Cleaning and lightly oiling metal tool parts after use prevents rust and corrosion, keeping tools functional and extending their lifespan.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A tractor on a modern farm serves mainly as a source of
options: irrigation water for crops
storage for harvested produce
chemical for pest control
power for pulling and operating various farm implements
questions.explanation: The tractor is the primary mobile power unit on mechanised farms, used to pull or drive implements such as ploughs, harrows, and planters.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A bulldozer is commonly used on the farm mainly for
options: measuring soil pH
milking dairy cattle
clearing land of trees, stumps, and debris before cultivation
spraying insecticides on growing crops
questions.explanation: The bulldozer's powerful blade pushes aside trees, stumps, and debris, making it useful for clearing virgin land before farming begins.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A sheller is a farm machine used mainly to
options: remove grains such as maize from the cob or pod
measure rainfall on the farm
spray fungicide on crops
plough and turn over the soil
questions.explanation: A sheller mechanically separates grains (e.g., maize kernels) from the cob, speeding up post-harvest processing compared to manual shelling.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A mist-blower is a piece of farm equipment used mainly for
options: applying pesticides in the form of a fine mist over crops
harvesting root and tuber crops
digging irrigation channels
measuring the moisture content of grain
questions.explanation: A mist-blower generates a fine spray or mist of pesticide, allowing even coverage over crop foliage for effective pest or disease control.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A knapsack sprayer is mainly used on the farm to
options: measure the depth of the water table
harvest cereal crops
apply liquid chemicals such as herbicides and insecticides to crops
till and prepare the seedbed
questions.explanation: The knapsack sprayer, carried on the back, is a manually operated device used to apply pesticides, herbicides, or foliar fertilisers to crops.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The mouldboard plough is used mainly for
options: spraying fungicide on standing crops
secondary tillage to pulverise soil clods
harvesting mature grain crops
primary tillage, cutting and turning over the soil
questions.explanation: The mouldboard plough cuts a furrow and turns the soil slice over, burying weeds and crop residue as part of primary tillage.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A disc plough is preferred over a mouldboard plough mainly for use in
options: nursery seedbeds only
very wet, sticky clay soils only
hard, dry, or stony soils, and areas with root debris
flower gardens only
questions.explanation: Disc ploughs, with their rotating discs, can cut through hard, dry, stony, or root-filled soils more effectively than a mouldboard plough.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A disc harrow is mainly used for
options: harvesting root crops
applying fertiliser in bands
secondary tillage, breaking clods into a finer tilth after ploughing
primary tillage to break virgin land
questions.explanation: The disc harrow follows primary ploughing, further breaking down large soil clods to prepare a fine seedbed for planting.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A ridger, whether animal-drawn or tractor-mounted, is used mainly to
options: measure soil temperature
spray herbicide over a wide field
form ridges or mounds in preparation for planting certain crops
harvest mature cereal crops
questions.explanation: Ridging creates raised soil ridges that improve drainage and aeration, commonly used before planting crops such as yam, cassava, or maize.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A planter, as a piece of farm machinery, is designed mainly to
options: harvest mature crops from the field
remove weeds from between crop rows
spray fertiliser onto the leaves of crops
place seeds at the correct depth and spacing in the soil
questions.explanation: Planters mechanically sow seeds at a controlled depth and spacing, improving planting accuracy and speed compared to manual planting.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A combine harvester is designed to perform which combination of operations simultaneously?
options: Planting, weeding, and irrigating
Cutting (reaping), threshing, and cleaning of grain crops
Milking, feeding, and housing livestock
Ploughing, harrowing, and ridging
questions.explanation: A combine harvester performs several harvesting operations at once, cutting the crop, separating the grain (threshing), and cleaning it, in a single pass.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The internal combustion engine, which powers most tractors, generates power mainly by
options: using wind to rotate a turbine
using stored chemical energy in a battery alone
burning fuel within cylinders to drive pistons
converting solar energy directly into mechanical motion
questions.explanation: In an internal combustion engine, fuel is ignited and burned inside the cylinders, and the resulting expanding gases drive the pistons that generate mechanical power.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The piston in an internal combustion engine functions mainly to
options: cool the engine during operation
filter impurities from the engine oil
store fuel before combustion
move up and down within the cylinder, transmitting the force of combustion to the crankshaft
questions.explanation: The piston is driven by the force of the burning fuel-air mixture, and its reciprocating motion is converted into rotary motion by the crankshaft.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The crankshaft in an internal combustion engine functions mainly to
options: filter air entering the engine
convert the reciprocating motion of the pistons into rotary motion
cool the engine cylinders
supply fuel to the combustion chamber
questions.explanation: The crankshaft transforms the up-and-down (reciprocating) movement of the pistons into the rotary motion needed to drive the wheels or power take-off.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Human power, as a source of farm power, is characterised mainly by
options: complete independence from fatigue or rest
extremely high output suited only to very large farms
relatively low output but flexibility for precise, small-scale tasks
zero cost of maintenance
questions.explanation: Human labour, while limited in power output compared to machines, offers flexibility and precision valuable for tasks like weeding, planting, and harvesting on small farms.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Animal power, such as from oxen or donkeys, is commonly used on farms mainly to
options: generate electricity for farm buildings
power irrigation pumps directly
pull simple implements such as ploughs and carts
spray chemicals over large fields
questions.explanation: Draught animals like oxen and donkeys provide a renewable power source for pulling basic implements, especially where mechanised power is limited.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Mechanical power, such as from tractors and engines, is valued on farms mainly because it
options: is always cheaper to acquire than a hoe
requires no fuel or maintenance
can only be used for very small-scale farming
performs farm operations faster and with greater output than human or animal power
questions.explanation: Mechanical power sources, like tractor engines, can perform tasks such as ploughing and harvesting far more quickly and on a larger scale than manual or animal power.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Electrical power on a farm is commonly used mainly for
options: pulling primary tillage implements in the field
fixing atmospheric nitrogen in the soil
harvesting standing crops directly
running processing equipment, lighting, and pumps
questions.explanation: Electricity is typically used to power stationary equipment such as grinders, incubators, irrigation pumps, and lighting on the farm.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Solar power, as an alternative farm power source, is valued mainly because it
options: harnesses sunlight to provide renewable energy for pumps and other equipment
generates significant noise pollution
requires burning fossil fuels continuously
only works effectively at night
questions.explanation: Solar power converts sunlight into electricity or heat, offering farmers a renewable, environmentally friendly energy source, especially in remote areas.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Wind power, as a farm energy source, is harnessed mainly through the use of
options: internal combustion engines
hydroelectric dams
solar panels
windmills or wind turbines that convert wind energy into mechanical or electrical power
questions.explanation: Windmills and wind turbines capture the kinetic energy of moving air and convert it into mechanical or electrical power for tasks like pumping water.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A farmstead survey is best described as the
options: process of examining and measuring farmland to plan the layout of farm buildings and facilities
process of applying fertiliser to a field
harvesting of mature crops from the farm
breeding of improved livestock varieties
questions.explanation: A farmstead survey involves assessing and measuring the land to guide the efficient planning and positioning of farm buildings, roads, and other facilities.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A ranging pole, used in farmstead surveying, is mainly used to
options: mark points and align straight lines across the field during measurement
measure the exact angle between two lines
dig planting holes for seedlings
spray chemicals over a marked area
questions.explanation: Ranging poles are set up as visible markers at intervals, helping surveyors sight straight lines and mark reference points accurately.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A measuring tape, used in farmstead surveying, is mainly used to
options: measure distances between points on the farmland
determine the slope angle of the land
measure rainfall intensity
test the pH of the soil
questions.explanation: Measuring tapes provide a direct, practical means of measuring linear distances between survey points on farmland.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A Gunter's chain, a traditional surveying tool, is mainly used to
options: measure wind speed on the farm
determine the vertical angle of a slope
test soil moisture content
measure distances on land during a survey
questions.explanation: The Gunter's chain, made of linked metal segments of standard length, is a traditional tool used specifically for measuring distances in land surveying.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A prism, used in modern surveying instruments, functions mainly to
options: store survey data electronically
cut vegetation along the survey line
reflect and redirect light for accurate sighting and measurement
measure the temperature of the soil
questions.explanation: Prisms reflect light back to surveying instruments such as theodolites or total stations, enabling precise distance and angle measurements.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A theodolite is a surveying instrument used mainly to
options: apply fertiliser to crops
measure the moisture content of the soil
measure horizontal and vertical angles accurately
till and prepare the seedbed
questions.explanation: The theodolite is a precision optical instrument used to measure both horizontal and vertical angles, essential for accurate land surveying.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: When selecting a site for farm buildings, an important consideration is that the site should
options: be as far as possible from any water source
have no consideration for wind direction
have good drainage and be easily accessible by road
be located in a waterlogged, low-lying area
questions.explanation: A good farm building site should drain well to avoid flooding and be conveniently accessible for transporting produce, inputs, and workers.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: In farmstead layout planning, livestock housing should ideally be positioned
options: downwind and at a reasonable distance from the farmhouse to reduce odour and disease risk
without any consideration of drainage
directly beside the farmhouse regardless of wind direction
on the steepest slope available
questions.explanation: Placing livestock housing downwind and at a suitable distance from the farmhouse helps minimise odour nuisance and the risk of disease transmission to the household.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Farmstead planning should ensure that farm roads and pathways are laid out mainly to
options: allow easy and efficient movement of people, produce, and machinery around the farm
be located only at the farm boundary
maximise the distance between the farmhouse and all other structures
prevent any vehicle access to the farm
questions.explanation: Well-planned farm roads and paths ensure efficient movement of labour, inputs, machinery, and produce between different parts of the farmstead.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Crops that complete their life cycle (from germination to seed production and death) within one growing season are called
options: annuals
perennials
biennials
epiphytes
questions.explanation: Annual crops such as maize and rice germinate, grow, flower, produce seed, and die within a single season or year.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A crop that requires two growing seasons to complete its life cycle, typically producing vegetative growth in the first year and flowering/seeding in the second, is called a
options: annual
climber
biennial
perennial
questions.explanation: Biennial crops, such as cabbage grown for seed, complete their life cycle over two seasons, storing food in the first year and reproducing in the second.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Crops such as cocoa, oil palm, and citrus, which live and produce for many years, are classified as
options: perennials
ephemerals
annuals
biennials
questions.explanation: Perennial crops live for more than two years and continue to produce yields over many growing seasons, unlike annuals or biennials.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Based on economic use, maize, rice, and millet are classified as
options: fibre crops
legumes
beverage crops
cereals
questions.explanation: Cereals are cultivated grasses grown mainly for their edible grains and form the staple food base for much of the world's population.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Cowpea, groundnut, and soybean are classified economically as
options: cereals
legumes
root and tuber crops
spice crops
questions.explanation: Legumes belong to the family Fabaceae and are valued both as protein-rich food crops and for their ability to fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Yam, cassava, and cocoyam are grouped together economically as
options: beverage crops
root and tuber crops
fibre crops
cereal crops
questions.explanation: Root and tuber crops are cultivated primarily for their starchy underground storage organs, which serve as major sources of carbohydrates.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Cotton, jute, and kenaf are examples of crops classified economically as
options: latex crops
oil crops
spice crops
fibre crops
questions.explanation: Fibre crops are grown for the strong plant fibres they yield, which are processed into textiles, ropes, and sacking materials.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Oil palm, groundnut, and coconut are classified economically as
options: oil crops
cereal crops
beverage crops
fibre crops
questions.explanation: Oil crops are cultivated mainly for the extraction of vegetable oils from their seeds or fruits, used for cooking and industrial purposes.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Cocoa, coffee, and kola are examples of crops classified economically as
options: fibre crops
beverage crops
cereal crops
root crops
questions.explanation: Beverage crops are grown mainly for processing into drinks such as cocoa, coffee, and cola drinks, and are important cash/export crops in West Africa.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Ginger, pepper, and clove are examples of crops classified economically as
options: fibre crops
cereal crops
spice crops
legume crops
questions.explanation: Spice crops are cultivated for their aromatic or pungent plant parts used to flavour and season food.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Rubber is a crop grown mainly for its
options: protein-rich seeds
aromatic leaves used as spice
edible starchy tubers
latex, which is processed into rubber products
questions.explanation: Rubber trees are tapped for their milky latex, which is coagulated and processed into natural rubber for tyres and other products.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the basis for classifying crops into annuals, biennials, and perennials?
options: The crop's family classification
The crop's economic use
The length of the crop's life cycle
The colour of the crop's flowers
questions.explanation: Classification into annuals, biennials, and perennials is based purely on how long the crop takes to complete its life cycle, not its use or botanical family.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is classified as a monocotyledonous crop?
options: Groundnut
Cowpea
Cocoa
Maize
questions.explanation: Maize, like other cereals, is a monocotyledon with one seed leaf (cotyledon), parallel leaf veins, and a fibrous root system.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is classified as a dicotyledonous crop?
options: Rice
Cowpea
Maize
Millet
questions.explanation: Cowpea, a legume, is a dicotyledon with two seed leaves, net-veined leaves, and typically a taproot system.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Sugarcane is classified economically as a
options: spice crop
fibre crop
sugar crop
legume crop
questions.explanation: Sugarcane is cultivated primarily for its sucrose-rich stem juice, which is processed into sugar and other sweeteners.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Site selection for crop production should mainly take into consideration
options: the colour of the surrounding vegetation only
the political affiliation of nearby farmers
soil fertility, topography, drainage, and accessibility
the distance from the farmer's house alone
questions.explanation: A suitable site must have fertile, well-drained soil, manageable slope, and good access for input supply and produce evacuation.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Land preparation for crop production typically begins with
options: application of fertiliser
planting of seeds
harvesting of the previous crop
clearing of existing vegetation
questions.explanation: Clearing removes existing bush, trees, and debris from the site, providing the first step before ploughing, harrowing, and planting.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Rice can be propagated by
options: budding only
grafting only
stem cuttings only
direct seeding or transplanting of seedlings
questions.explanation: Rice is commonly established either by sowing seeds directly in the field (direct seeding) or by raising seedlings in a nursery and transplanting them.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Cassava is normally propagated using
options: grafting
true seeds
seedlings from a nursery
stem cuttings
questions.explanation: Cassava is vegetatively propagated from mature stem cuttings, which root and sprout quickly, unlike crops raised from true seed.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Yam is commonly propagated by planting
options: grafted scions
true botanical seeds
setts (portions of the tuber)
leaf cuttings
questions.explanation: Yam is vegetatively propagated using setts, which are cut portions of seed yams, since true seed propagation is rarely used commercially.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The recommended planting depth and spacing for a crop are mainly determined by the
options: market price of the produce
seed size and growth habit of the crop
colour of the seed coat
religion of the farmer
questions.explanation: Larger seeds are generally planted deeper, and spacing is set to match the crop's mature size and growth habit to avoid overcrowding or wasted land.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: The correct time to plant a rain-fed crop is best determined by the
options: colour of the soil
availability of storage facilities alone
onset and reliability of the rainy season
market price of the crop at harvest
questions.explanation: Planting date for rain-fed crops is timed to coincide with the reliable onset of rains to ensure adequate moisture for germination and growth.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Seed rate refers to the
options: rate at which seeds germinate
cost of seeds per bag
speed of seed dispersal by wind
quantity of seed required to plant a given area of land
questions.explanation: Seed rate is the amount of seed needed per unit area, calculated based on spacing, germination percentage, and desired plant population.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Weeding in crop production is carried out mainly to
options: increase the number of pests in the field
prevent the crop from flowering
remove unwanted plants competing with the crop for resources
reduce soil fertility
questions.explanation: Weeding removes plants that compete with the crop for light, water, nutrients, and space, thereby improving crop growth and yield.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Thinning in crop production refers to the
options: removal of excess seedlings to leave the required plant population
addition of extra seeds to a stand
removal of weeds from the field
application of fertiliser to young seedlings
questions.explanation: Thinning reduces overcrowded seedlings within a stand to the recommended number per stand, reducing competition and improving growth of the remaining plants.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Supplying, as a crop management practice, refers to
options: harvesting mature crops
replacing seeds or seedlings that failed to germinate or establish
removing excess seedlings from a stand
applying fertiliser to the crop
questions.explanation: Supplying fills in gaps left by seeds that failed to germinate or seedlings that died, ensuring a full and even plant population.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A basal fertiliser application is applied
options: only at harvest
only after the crop has flowered
at or before planting, to supply nutrients for early growth
only to control weeds
questions.explanation: Basal fertiliser is worked into the soil at or before planting to make nutrients available to the crop from the earliest growth stages.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: A top-dressing fertiliser application is applied
options: before land preparation
during the growing season, usually around the crop
only to seeds before sowing
after the crop has been harvested and stored
questions.explanation: Top-dressing supplies additional nutrients, especially nitrogen, to a growing crop by applying fertiliser on or around the soil surface near the plants.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Rice is typically harvested when the
options: grains have turned golden-brown and hardened
plant has just started flowering
plant is still at the seedling stage
field has just been flooded for transplanting
questions.explanation: Rice is ready for harvest once the grains mature, changing colour from green to golden-brown and hardening, indicating physiological maturity.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Maize cobs are generally harvested when the
options: husks turn brown/dry and the grains have hardened
silk first appears on the cob
tassels have not yet emerged
plant is only knee-high
questions.explanation: Maize is harvested at physiological maturity, indicated by browning, drying husks and hardened grains with a black layer at the grain base.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Cassava tubers are generally ready for harvesting between
options: 2 and 3 days after planting
8 and 18 months after planting, depending on the variety
24 hours after flowering
1 and 2 weeks after planting
questions.explanation: Cassava tubers mature over an extended period, and harvesting time varies by variety, typically ranging from about 8 months to 18 months after planting.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Yam tubers are generally harvested when the
options: vines turn yellow and begin to dry up
field has just been irrigated
vines are still green and actively growing
seed yams have just been planted
questions.explanation: Yellowing and drying of the yam vine signals that the tuber has reached maturity and is ready for harvesting.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Cowpea pods are harvested when they
options: are still green and immature
turn brown/dry and begin to split
have just flowered
are still underground
questions.explanation: Mature cowpea pods dry and turn brown, sometimes beginning to split, indicating that the seeds inside are ready for harvest.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Groundnut is generally ready for harvest when the
options: leaves turn yellow and the pods show a firm, veined inner shell
plant is still flowering
seedlings have just emerged
pods are still white and soft
questions.explanation: Groundnut maturity is judged by yellowing leaves and pods that show darkened veins and a hardened inner shell when opened.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Cocoa pods are harvested when they
options: first begin to flower
have just been planted as seedlings
are still small and green
change colour from green to yellow or orange/red, depending on variety
questions.explanation: Cocoa pod ripeness is judged by a change in pod colour, from green to yellow or orange-red depending on the variety, signalling readiness for harvest.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Oil palm fruit bunches are harvested when the
options: spikelets have just opened as flowers
bunch is still entirely green
fruits turn reddish-orange and some begin to detach naturally
palm is less than one year old
questions.explanation: Ripe oil palm bunches show a reddish-orange fruit colour, and loose fruits detaching naturally indicate the bunch is ready for harvest.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Processing of harvested cassava into garri mainly involves
options: peeling, grating, fermenting, dewatering, sieving, and frying
simply drying the whole tuber in the sun
storing the tuber underground indefinitely
boiling the tuber whole and eating immediately
questions.explanation: Garri processing involves several steps: peeling and grating the tuber, fermenting the mash, pressing out excess water, sieving, and frying to produce the finished product.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Proper storage of harvested grains such as maize and rice mainly requires
options: leaving the grains exposed to rain
drying to a safe moisture content before storage in pest-proof containers
storing without any pest control measures
storing while still wet and undried
questions.explanation: Grains must be dried to a low, safe moisture content to prevent mould growth, and stored in structures protected from pests and rodents.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Yam tubers are commonly stored using the
options: yam barn (a raised, well-ventilated structure)
cold-room method only
storage in sealed airtight tins
underwater storage method
questions.explanation: Traditional yam barns provide shade and ventilation, allowing air to circulate around tubers tied to a frame, reducing rot and sprouting during storage.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Which of the following is an important consideration when selecting a site for establishing a cocoa or oil palm plantation?
options: Presence of extremely low annual rainfall
Proximity to a desert region
Availability of only rocky, shallow soils
Availability of adequate rainfall and suitable forest/derived-savanna soils
questions.explanation: Cocoa and oil palm require high, well-distributed rainfall and deep, fertile soils typical of rainforest or derived-savanna zones for good establishment and yield.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Land preparation for yam cultivation commonly involves the construction of
options: flat seedbeds only, with no ridging
mounds or ridges
deep trenches for flooding
raised concrete platforms
questions.explanation: Yam is typically planted on mounds or ridges, which provide loose, well-aerated soil that allows the tuber to expand and develop properly.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: One of the main aims of crop improvement is to develop varieties with
options: increased susceptibility to disease
longer maturity periods with lower yield
higher yield and resistance to pests and diseases
smaller root systems and weaker stems
questions.explanation: Crop improvement programmes aim to combine desirable traits such as higher yield, disease/pest resistance, and better quality into new varieties.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Early maturity is a desirable trait targeted in crop improvement mainly because it
options: eliminates the need for fertiliser application
prevents the crop from ever flowering
always reduces the total yield of the crop
allows farmers to harvest sooner and often escape late-season pests, diseases, or drought
questions.explanation: Early-maturing varieties can be harvested before the onset of adverse conditions like drought or heavy pest/disease pressure late in the season, and allow more cropping cycles per year.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Selection, as a method of crop improvement, involves
options: crossing two different plant varieties
randomly mixing seeds without regard to traits
introducing an entirely new crop species from another region
choosing and propagating plants with the most desirable characteristics from an existing population
questions.explanation: Selection identifies naturally occurring plants with superior traits within an existing population and propagates them to gradually improve the crop.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Hybridisation in crop improvement refers to the
options: planting of a crop in a new geographic area
process of selecting the tallest plants in a field
harvesting of seeds from only one parent plant
deliberate crossing of two genetically different parent plants to combine desirable traits
questions.explanation: Hybridisation combines the genetic material of two different parents through controlled crossing, aiming to produce offspring with a combination of desirable characteristics.

questions.subject: Agricultural Science
questions.text: Introduction, as a method of crop improvement, involves
options: crossing two plants of the same variety
